snip.t: | Heart failure (pulmonary oedema) | Orthopnoea, peripheral oedema, elevated JVP, bibasal crackles, rapid onset dyspnoea | BNP elevated, chest X‑ray shows Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly; cough is usually dry, not productive mucus‑laden |
Pulmonary interstitium – loose connective tissue, lymphatics, capillaries: Inflammatory oedema expands the interstitium, producing crackles on auscultation and increasing the work of breathing.
Pulmonary circulation – low‑pressure, high‑flow system: Inflammation increases vascular permeability → pulmonary oedema; septic emboli can seed additional lobes, explaining multilobar disease.
Therapeutic aspiration for symptom relief (ultrasound-guided, stop at about 1.5 L or when the patient coughs or has chest tightness, to avoid re-expansion pulmonary oedema).
Empyema, pleural thickening and fibrosis (trapped lung), respiratory failure, re-expansion pulmonary oedema, pneumothorax and bleeding from aspiration.

Tension pneumothorax and cardiac arrest, persistent air leak (bronchopleural fistula), re-expansion pulmonary oedema, infection (empyema), recurrence (about 30% after a first primary episode), haemopneumothorax, surgical emphysema.
Bronchoconstriction (smooth muscle spasm), mucosal oedema, mucus plugging.

qs.q: A patient suddenly becomes severely breathless with an SpO2 below 90% and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates during a blood transfusion. The patient has a normal JVP, no peripheral oedema, and normal blood pressure. What is the appropriate initial management?
o: Stop the transfusion and administer IV furosemide immediately
Stop the transfusion and provide high-flow oxygen support
Slow the transfusion rate and administer prophylactic drugs
Continue the transfusion under observation with adrenaline
qs.e: The clinical presentation describes TRALI, an immune-mediated lung reaction characterized by non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema where diuretics will worsen the condition. Management involves stopping the transfusion and providing respiratory support without diuretics.
qs.s: Blood Transfusion Contraindications & Acute Reactions: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with chronic heart failure develops hypertension, tachycardia, raised jugular venous pressure, and peripheral oedema halfway through a red blood cell transfusion. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Administer packed red cells alongside fluid boluses
Stop the transfusion and administer IV furosemide
Stop the transfusion and administer IV adrenaline
Continue the transfusion slowly while giving oxygen
qs.e: This patient is experiencing Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload, which presents with hypertension and signs of volume overload requiring cessation of transfusion and loop diuretics. Adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis, not hydrostatic pulmonary oedema.
qs.s: Blood Transfusion Contraindications & Acute Reactions: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old presents with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, generalized oedema, and hyperlipidaemia. Which of the following clinical syndromes best matches this constellation of findings?
o: chronic kidney disease
nephrotic syndrome
nephritic syndrome
rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
qs.e: The defining manifestations of nephrotic syndrome include proteinuria greater than 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia, and lipiduria. Nephritic syndrome is classically characterized by haematuria, red cell casts, and hypertension.
qs.s: Glomerular Diseases: Classification, Histology & Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: Which set of findings points directly to pulmonary oedema on a chest X-ray?
o: Focal consolidation and air bronchograms
Hyperinflation and flat diaphragms
Pleural line and absent lung markings
Cardiomegaly and Kerley B lines
qs.e: Cardiomegaly, perihilar shadowing, and Kerley B lines are typical findings of pulmonary oedema related to heart failure. Hyperinflation and flat diaphragms are seen in COPD.
qs.s: Chest X-ray Interpretation Guide: ABCDE Approach for Medical Students: MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old patient with advanced COPD presents with peripheral oedema and morning headaches. Which underlying physiological abnormality is most strongly suggested by these symptoms?
o: Isolated left ventricular failure associated with fluid retention
Acute renal tubular necrosis presenting with electrolyte loss
Severe chronic hypercapnia affecting renal excretion processes
Primary hyperparathyroidism causing systemic generalized edema
qs.e: In advanced disease, oedema and morning headaches may suggest hypercapnia. Oedema usually relates to the failure of salt and water excretion by the hypoxic, hypercapnic kidney.

qs.q: During the evaluation of a patient with advanced COPD, peripheral oedema is observed. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism responsible for this physical sign?
o: Failure of salt and water excretion by the hypoxic, hypercapnic kidney
Direct mechanical compression of the inferior vena cava by hyperinflated lungs
Severe systemic arterial hypotension leading to aldosterone upregulation
Primary hepatic cirrhosis secondary to chronic alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
qs.e: Oedema usually relates to failure of salt and water excretion by the hypoxic, hypercapnic kidney. It is not caused by inferior vena cava compression or primary hepatic cirrhosis.

qs.q: A recipient develops hypotension and respiratory distress presenting as non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within six hours of a blood transfusion. Which reaction has most likely occurred?
o: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction
Transfusion-related acute lung injury
Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction
qs.e: TRALI is characterized by hypotension and respiratory distress caused by donor anti-leucocyte antibodies reacting against recipient white blood cells. TACO involves volume overload and presents with hypertension rather than hypotension.
qs.s: Blood Transfusion Guide: ABO, Reactions, Products & Safety: MCQs

qs.q: What is the maximum volume of pleural fluid that is advised not to exceed during a single therapeutic aspiration to avoid re-expansion pulmonary oedema?
o: Not exceeding 1.5 L of pleural fluid
Not exceeding 0.5 L of pleural fluid
Not exceeding 2.0 L of pleural fluid
Not exceeding 1.0 L of pleural fluid
qs.e: Removing more than 1.5 L of pleural fluid in one episode is inadvisable due to a small risk of re-expansion pulmonary oedema. Smaller volumes are safer for palliating breathlessness.

ai.summary: Oedema is the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space, leading to swelling. It can be localized or generalized, often indicating an underlying medical condition. Understanding its cause is crucial for effective clinical management.

sections.p: Oedema is defined as an excessive accumulation of fluid in the interstitial tissue spaces. It manifests as visible swelling and can be diagnosed clinically through physical examination, observing for swelling, skin changes, and assessing for pitting.
b: Pitting oedema: Indentation remains after pressure is applied, indicating fluid is easily displaced.
Non-pitting oedema: No indentation remains, often seen in lymphatic obstruction or thyroid disease.
Localized oedema: Confined to a specific area, e.g., an ankle or a limb.
Generalized oedema (anasarca): Widespread swelling affecting multiple body parts, including ankle/sacral swelling.

sections.p: Oedema severity is primarily assessed by its extent and the degree of pitting. While no universal staging system exists, clinical assessment helps guide management and monitor response to treatment.
b: Mild oedema: Localized, often at ankles, resolves with elevation.
Moderate oedema: More widespread, affecting lower limbs, sacrum, or abdomen.
Severe oedema (anasarca): Generalized swelling, including face, upper limbs, and body cavities, indicating significant fluid overload.
Pitting depth: Often graded +1 (slight indentation) to +4 (deep indentation lasting over 30 seconds).
Unilateral leg oedema: Calf circumference more than 3 cm larger than the other side (measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity) suggests significant swelling, as seen in DVT.

sections.p: Oedema results from an imbalance in Starling forces across capillary walls, leading to increased fluid filtration or impaired lymphatic drainage. Identifying the underlying cause is paramount for effective treatment.
b: Increased hydrostatic pressure (e.g., Congestive Cardiac Failure (CCF), constrictive pericarditis, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), venous insufficiency).
Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (e.g., Nephrotic syndrome, liver cirrhosis, severe malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy).
Increased capillary permeability (e.g., Inflammation, allergic reactions, sepsis, burns, angioedema).
Lymphatic obstruction (e.g., Filariasis, surgery, radiation, malignancy, congenital lymphedema).
Renal causes (e.g., Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN), renal failure).
Hepatic causes (e.g., Liver cirrhosis, hepatoma, liver failure).
Medication side effects (e.g., Calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs, corticosteroids).

sections.p: The presentation of oedema varies depending on its cause and location, ranging from localized swelling to life-threatening systemic fluid overload.
b: Generalized oedema: Bilateral ankle/sacral swelling, facial puffiness, abdominal distension (ascites), weight gain.
Unilateral leg oedema: Calf or leg pain, swelling, tenderness, warmth, redness, pitting oedema, dilated superficial collateral veins (suggestive of DVT).
Pulmonary oedema: Shortness of breath, cough, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, chest tightness.
Airway oedema: Stridor, hoarseness, difficulty breathing due to mucosal oedema (e.g., in anaphylaxis).
Cerebral oedema: Headache, altered mental status, seizures, focal neurological deficits.
Skin changes: Taut, shiny skin, sometimes with hyperpigmentation or ulceration in chronic cases.

sections.p: Investigations aim to identify the underlying cause and assess the severity and impact of oedema, guiding targeted management.

t.b: What is the likely cause, extent, and duration of oedema? -> Clinical signs (pitting, location, associated symptoms like dyspnoea, pain) help narrow down differential diagnoses. In low-resource settings, this is often the primary diagnostic tool.
Is there anaemia or infection? -> Anaemia can worsen cardiac function; elevated white cells suggest infection/inflammation.
Is there renal dysfunction or electrolyte imbalance? -> Elevated creatinine suggests renal failure; hyponatraemia can be seen in severe CCF or SIADH.
Is there hepatic dysfunction or hypoalbuminaemia? -> Elevated LFTs suggest liver disease; low albumin is a key feature of nephrotic syndrome and liver failure.

Is there cardiac dysfunction (e.g., CCF, constrictive pericarditis)? -> ECG shows arrhythmias or ischaemia; echocardiogram assesses cardiac structure and function (ejection fraction, valvular disease).

t.a: D-dimer, Doppler Ultrasound of affected limb
t.b: Is there a Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)? -> Elevated D-dimer suggests clot formation; ultrasound directly visualizes thrombi. If ultrasound is unavailable, clinical probability scores (e.g., Wells' score) are used.
Is there pulmonary oedema or pleural effusion? -> Cardiomegaly, Kerley B lines, and blunting of costophrenic angles suggest fluid overload in the lungs.

sections.p: Certain presentations of oedema signal severe underlying conditions or immediate life-threatening complications requiring urgent medical intervention.
b: Rapidly worsening generalized oedema or anasarca, indicating severe organ dysfunction.
Acute shortness of breath, cough, or chest tightness, suggesting pulmonary oedema or pleural effusion.
Stridor or difficulty swallowing, indicating airway oedema and potential obstruction.
Unilateral leg oedema with pain and warmth, raising suspicion for DVT and risk of pulmonary embolism.
Altered mental status or neurological deficits, potentially due to cerebral oedema.
Skin breakdown, cellulitis, or ulceration over oedematous areas, leading to infection.
Re-expansion pulmonary oedema after rapid drainage of large pleural effusions or ascites.

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause, reducing fluid overload, and preventing complications. The approach varies significantly based on the aetiology.
b: Treat the underlying cause: Address CCF with appropriate medications, manage renal or liver failure, treat infections, or remove offending drugs.
Diuretics (e.g., furosemide): To increase renal excretion of sodium and water, reducing fluid overload in conditions like CCF or renal failure.
Fluid and sodium restriction: To limit further fluid accumulation, especially in cardiac or renal oedema.
Elevation of affected limbs: To promote venous and lymphatic drainage, reducing localized swelling.
Compression therapy (e.g., stockings): To reduce swelling in chronic venous insufficiency or lymphedema.

Therapeutic aspiration (e.g., paracentesis for ascites, thoracentesis for pleural effusion): For symptom relief, guided by ultrasound, stopping at about 1.5 L or when the patient coughs or has chest tightness to avoid re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
Albumin infusion: In severe hypoalbuminaemia (e.g., nephrotic syndrome, liver failure) to increase oncotic pressure, often combined with diuretics.
Surgical intervention: Timing for clean surgical injury oedema is early (within days); for chronic inflammation or slough, repair waits until oedema settles (about 2-3 months).

sections.p: Long-term management involves monitoring the patient's condition, adherence to treatment, and lifestyle modifications to prevent recurrence and manage chronic oedema.
b: Regular clinical assessment: Monitor weight, oedema severity, and vital signs.
Adherence to medications: Ensure consistent use of diuretics, cardiac medications, or other prescribed treatments.
Dietary modifications: Maintain low-sodium diet, especially in cardiac or renal oedema.
Lifestyle changes: Regular exercise, elevation of legs, and avoiding prolonged standing or sitting.
Management of underlying conditions: Strict control of chronic diseases like heart failure, kidney disease, or liver disease.
Skin care: Protect oedematous skin from injury and infection.

sections.p: It's important to differentiate oedema from other forms of swelling or tissue enlargement that may appear similar but have different underlying causes and management.
b: Lipoedema: Symmetrical fat accumulation, primarily in legs and thighs, often painful, non-pitting, and spares the feet.
Cellulitis: Localized skin infection characterized by redness, warmth, tenderness, and swelling, but less likely to be pitting.
Hematoma: Localized collection of blood outside blood vessels, typically firm and discolored.
Tumors or cysts: Localized masses that are typically non-pitting and have distinct borders.
Myxoedema: Non-pitting swelling, especially of the face and hands, due to deposition of mucopolysaccharides in hypothyroidism.

sections.p: Clinical signs and laboratory results related to oedema can sometimes be misleading, requiring careful interpretation in the context of the patient's overall clinical picture.
b: Early oedema may not be clinically apparent, especially in obese patients, until significant fluid retention has occurred.
Dehydration can mask oedema, as fluid shifts may not be evident despite underlying fluid retention.
Normal laboratory values (e.g., albumin) do not rule out localized oedema due to inflammation or venous obstruction.
Diuretic use can normalize electrolyte levels temporarily, masking underlying renal or cardiac dysfunction.
False negative D-dimer in DVT can occur in patients with symptoms for several days or on anticoagulants.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset or rapidly worsening oedema
Shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, or chest pain
Unilateral leg swelling with pain, warmth, or redness
Altered mental status or severe headache

faq.a: Pitting oedema is swelling that leaves a temporary indentation or 'pit' when pressure is applied to the affected area, indicating the presence of excess interstitial fluid that can be displaced.
Yes, oedema can be painful, especially if it develops rapidly, is severe, or is associated with inflammation, infection (e.g., cellulitis), or conditions like deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
No, not all swelling is oedema. Swelling can also be caused by fat accumulation (lipoedema), blood clots (hematoma), tumors, cysts, or inflammation without significant fluid accumulation.
